commits.subject: fix(cli): describe one-shot timeouts for an invocation whose session has ended (#8535)
commits.body:
fix(cli): describe one-shot timeouts for an invocation whose session has ended (#8535)

* fix(cli): describe one-shot timeouts for an invocation whose session has ended

A one-shot CLI analysis that reached a provider deadline told its caller
that the Ghidra session remained usable and reported a runtime-editable
limit applying to the next operation, although the command had already
released its provider session and runtime.

The shared error projection now takes an explicit caller lifetime.
Providers keep guidance that holds only for a continuing caller (session
reuse, same-session runtime updates) apart from the request outcome, and
the presentation adds it only for a continuing caller. One-shot owners
(runDirectAnalysis, runProviderAnalysis, finishAnalysisCommand and the
JavaScript application command) project for the invocation: details.limit
reports scope rea-invocation, applies_at next_invocation and the launch
environment seed, and the remediation leads with that setting for a new
invocation. MCP output keeps its runtime-update and same-session guidance.

Covers the Ghidra decompile timeout, decompiler failure, regex stack
exhaustion and startup timeout, the shared regex deadline, the Kuna
decompile timeout and the Hopper startup timeout.

Fixes #8311

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): project composed child failures for the caller lifetime

Cleanup composition embedded its primary and cleanup failures as
continuing-caller projections, and baked the primary's message and the
cleanup's remediation into the composed error. A one-shot command whose
Ghidra startup timed out while shutdown also failed therefore still
reported a rea-runtime limit and update_analysis_settings in
details.diagnostics.primary_error.

childFailureDiagnostics now snapshots each embedded child at composition
for both lifetimes when its projection depends on the caller, so cleanup
history keeps its composition-time state and the final projection selects
the caller's form. composedCallerGuidance re-attributes message and
remediation with their continuing-only parts kept separate. Error copies
and redaction keep the invocation diagnostics. The Hopper startup timeout
now carries its continuing guidance on the error like the other producers.

Invocation limits keep agent_editable and rea_restart_required, with
values that hold for a new invocation, so only scope and applies_at
change and environment is added.

In existing-project mode a decompile timeout or a cancelled session now
says the next session copies and opens REA_GHIDRA_PROJECT_PATH again
rather than repeating import and analysis.

Tests compare delivered guidance with the owning formatters and constants
instead of freezing prose.

fix(setup): refuse Hopper on macOS below the release's minimum (#8548)

Hopper setup planning accepted any macOS 12+ host as supported, and the
installer never compared the host with the selected release. The current
publisher-signed Hopper 6.6.1-demo requires macOS 12.4 (feed

commits.subject: fix(process): re-read unreadable tokens before signaling and name the process (#8553)
commits.body:
fix(process): re-read unreadable tokens before signaling and name the process (#8553)

* fix(process): re-read unreadable tokens before signaling and name the process

Darwin KERN_PROCARGS2 samples a process's argument length and stack top
before it reads the address space, and exec publishes the new length
before it copies the new strings out (xnu sysctl_procargsx,
exec_copyout_strings). A read during exec can return a zero-filled or
stale strings area, and exec keeps the PID and start time that bracket
the read. The final sweep already re-read such tokens, but the
pre-signal group check read each member's token once, so one transient
read of a live group member failed the whole cleanup.

Move the bounded re-read into one shared fact-reading helper and use it
for both the sweep and the pre-signal group check. The group check binds
re-reads to the generation it first observed, so a reused PID stays
unresolved; the sweep keeps classifying the PID's current process.

An unreadable-token failure now carries the native identity read after
the token and the summary names the candidate by its native name,
parent, group and start identity. The Darwin helper and Linux procfs
reader report the short native process name (p_comm/comm) for display.

Fixes #8337

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(process): refresh other pre-signal members after token re-read waits

The pre-signal group check re-read only members whose token was
unavailable, so a readable member kept the relation it had before the
retry waits. A member that moved to another process group during those
waits could be validated on its old group, and the old group signaled
while the moved member kept running.

After any retry wait, the shared re-read helper now reads every other
live pre-signal fact once more with the same generation binding. A moved
member then takes the existing changed-group path, which retains its
ownership evidence and fails cleanup. An inconclusive refresh replaces
the stale fact so it fails closed. Nothing changes when no re-read ran,
and the sweep keeps classifying current processes because every group
it finds is revalidated before signaling.

Also cover PID reuse that happens before the re-read starts, where both
re-read identities agree and only the first-read generation rejects the
replacement's token.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(process): keep known identity changes final across token re-reads

The pre-signal re-read treated a first read without a same-generation
identity as unbound and replaced it with the re-read. On Linux the first
read can already establish PID reuse (an ESRCH token whose exit check sees
another generation); the re-read then classified the replacement, so a
zombie replacement could let cleanup succeed.

A pre-signal check now re-reads only same-generation facts. Changed,
exited, exiting and foreign-token facts are final. Each attempt also
re-reads the group's owned members instead of one separate refresh after
the loop, so a member that moves groups or turns unreadable while another
waits is seen within the same bound. The caller's run token selects the
owned members, and the sweep keeps classifying current processes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: fix(javascript): emit no event operation for a literal non-function listener (#8621)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): emit no event operation for a literal non-function listener (#8621)

* fix(javascript): emit no event operation for a literal non-function listener

`EventEmitter` validates a listener before registering or removing anything:

    if (typeof listener !== 'function')
      throw new ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE('listener', 'function', listener);

The throw is synchronous, before any listener exists, but the analysis reported a
`register` or `remove` operation for those calls.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    emitter.on(1)                      -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    emitter.on("x", 1)                 -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    emitter.on("x", null)              -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    emitter.on("x", true)              -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    emitter.on("x", {}) / ([])         -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    emitter.once / addListener / prependListener / prependOnceListener /
    off / removeListener with a literal -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    --- accepted ---
    emitter.on("x", () => {})          -> ok
    emitter.on("x", function () {})    -> ok

`rejectsEventListener` drops the operation only for an exactly readable literal
that cannot be a function. An identifier, a call result or a spread may still
supply a function and keeps its operation, and a class expression passes Node's
own `typeof` check.

`emit` and `removeAllListeners` are untouched: `emit` passes its remaining
arguments as data to listeners that already exist, and `removeAllListeners` takes
only an optional event name.

* fix(javascript): price a non-finite listener and keep a shifted spread

Two review findings on the event-listener guard.

**A non-finite numeric literal was missed.** Babel stores `1e999` as a
`NumericLiteral` holding `Infinity`, and the exact-value reader refuses to price a
non-finite number, so the guard never saw it:

    e.on("x", 1e999)  -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE

A numeric literal is always a number and therefore never callable, so the guard now
decides on the literal node directly.

**A leading spread shifts the listener position.** `e.on(...args, 1)` does not pass
`1` as the listener: Node spreads the array and ignores the trailing argument once
the listener is satisfied. The guard read `arguments[1]` regardless, so it dropped a
real registration. It now leaves the position undecided when argument 0 is a spread.

Five regressions cover both forms; all five fail without the fixes.

* fix(cli): keep captured source Evidence when one-shot delivery never commits

A completed observation that was cancelled at final close, failed cleanup, or
never reached bundle commit returned its evidence links but dropped the source
records the invocation had already captured. The caller could neither read those
records nor tell whether they were missing, captured or written.

Report the closure at publishCliAnalysisEvidence, the shared boundary every
--evidence_output command uses. details.source_closure carries authentic captured
records within 64 KiB and explicit omissions: not_captured for a link this
invocation holds no record for, and not_inlined for a captured record outside this
response. A committed bundle keeps its receipt instead, nothing is written after
cancellation, and successful delivery is unchanged.

* fix(cli): keep the typed failure when collecting source closure cannot finish

A captured source with a data-sized evidence_links array made
pending.push(...links) exceed V8's call-argument limit. On final-close
cancellation or a refused publication that RangeError replaced the original typed
failure, which is the one outcome this delivery step exists to preserve.

Walk the closure through a Set, which is a deduplicating breadth-first queue, so
no link becomes a call argument and each link costs one lookup however often it
repeats. undeliveredSourceClosure now owns authentication and never throws: if
examining the closure fails, it reports collection_failure with the bounded error
type and an unknown closure state, and the original failure is still returned.

Fault the final-close tests on the scope the command gave to matching, after
matching completed, and assert that close was reached, so a moved close fails
instead of passing on an earlier one.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): keep static facts after semantic results use the parent budget (#8648)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): keep static facts after semantic results use the parent budget (#8648)

Static checkpoints were admitted against the same budget as semantic and
application results, half of the parent's free heap. Once those charges used
it, the next checkpoint stopped the analysis and every remaining source lost
its static facts, with most of the parent heap still free.

Semantic and application results still stop at that budget. Static checkpoints
may now continue to three quarters of the free heap while the live heap also
has room for another copy of what it holds. Without that room, admission falls
back to the result budget. The live condition is needed because the limit V8
reports counts young-generation capacity that retained objects cannot use:
without it, the parent aborted on heap exhaustion at small heap limits.

Reserved relationships are given up only when the larger share runs short. A
stop still fails with a typed error, which now reports the limit that applied,
what was available, the live heap in use and what the checkpoint needed.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: fix(debugger): let REA exit when a debugger could not be stopped (#8652)
commits.body:
fix(debugger): let REA exit when a debugger could not be stopped (#8652)

* fix(debugger): let REA exit when a debugger could not be stopped

`rea debug-with-gdb` and `rea debug-with-rizin` printed cleanup_incomplete
and set exit status 1, but the retained child and its pipes kept the event
loop alive, so the process never exited. A stdio MCP server whose client
disconnected hung the same way.

closeOwnedDebuggerSessions is the owner both managers finish through. It now
unreferences retained sessions, as supervised providers already do after
incomplete cleanup, restores the references on retry, and names the retained
process IDs. The one-shot commands report those IDs, since no later command
can retry. Debugger ownership, signals and detach behavior are unchanged.

GDB cleanup requests also no longer hold the host until their 120 s command
deadline, because cleanup already bounds its own wait.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(debugger): name retained debuggers when an MCP server shuts down

An MCP server that exits with a retained debugger logged only "REA provider
cleanup failed" and "could not close cleanly", so nothing named the process
left for the caller to check. The PIDs were on OwnedDebuggerCleanupError, but
each shutdown reporter read only the outer aggregate's message, and the debug
failure_cause description dropped the field too.

The failure type now lives in its own dependency-free module with one reader
that walks composed failures. The shutdown report, the server's onclose log,
the debug description and the one-shot CLI all use it, and the shutdown report
writes the same remediation the CLI returns.

commits.subject: fix(native): select off-screen windows so the UI lane can complete (#8654)
commits.body:
fix(native): select off-screen windows so the UI lane can complete (#8654)

* fix(native): stop calling an off-screen window absent

The native UI helper looked up its selected window with
`.optionIncludingWindow`, which returned nothing while that window was off
screen. An existing window owned by the selected process was reported as
`window-mismatch`, before any permission check, so the verifier could not reach
its permission boundary. Select from all windows instead; absent and foreign
windows still fail.

The verifier's changed-bytes check also read `error.message`, but since
cc90771af a selection failure carries its helper code in `error.issues`, so the
check could not pass. Read the issue. Together these let the permissions lane
complete on main.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(native): own UI test processes from the moment they launch

The off-screen test registered cleanup only after parsing the ready record, so a
startup failure left `/usr/bin/open` and its app running. The lane test killed
only the verifier on a timeout, leaving its launcher and detached fixture alive
until they expired.

Register the off-screen owner immediately after the launch; the app inherits the
run token, so the sweep needs no ready record. In the lane test, every stand-in
records itself and leaves on one release the test's cleanup awaits.

commits.body:
fix(browser): keep negative script columns Chrome reports (#8684)

* fix(browser): keep negative script columns Chrome reports

Chrome reported a Debugger.scriptParsed event with startColumn -60 and
endColumn -15 for an inline script in WordPress's helper frame. CDP declares
these columns as plain integers, but REA's admission required min(0), so one
script failed the whole observe-web-execution run with unreadable_output.

CDP resource columns now share one representation, cdpResourceColumnSchema,
for script start/end columns, initiator call frames, parser initiators and
event listeners. Positions on a script's first line include its start column,
so keeping the reported values keeps the documented script-relative
conversion consistent. The domain contract and web runtime docs state that a
negative column does not locate a column in the resource.

Fixes #8674

* fix(browser): apply the CDP column policy to passive capture

inspect_web_page and discover_webmcp_tools still read CDP columns through
cdpSourceCoordinates, whose own >= 0 check turned a negative column into
null and reported invalid_protocol_value. WebMCP discovery also dropped the
tool's whole registration_source.

cdpResourceColumnSchema now lives with the domain's CDP observation schemas.
Runtime admission, the passive coordinate helper and the runtime, console,
initiator and WebMCP output schemas all use it. Lines keep their
non-negative rule.

feat(elf): decode Linux core dump process and memory mapping notes (#8830)

* feat(elf): decode Linux core dump process and memory mapping notes

Inspect Linux core dump note tables and decode structured metadata without
requiring external tools or debuggers:
- NT_PRPSINFO (type 3): decode process ID, parent ID, process group,
  session, UID, GID, execution state, filename, and command line arguments
  bounded by the text budget.
- NT_FILE (type 0x46494c45): decode mapped memory ranges (start_address,
  end_address, file_offset_pages) and mapped file paths with page size.
- NT_SIGINFO (type 0x53494749): decode faulting signal number, errno, and code.
- NT_AUXV (type 6): decode auxiliary vector pairs with known AT_* tag names.
- Support both 32-bit and 64-bit, little-endian and big-endian targets.
- Retain unknown core note types gracefully without partial success errors.
- Add comprehensive unit tests, fixtures, acceptance tests, and documentation.

commits.subject: fix(ghidra): mark empty xrefs results as unresolved, not unreferenced (#8831)
commits.body:
fix(ghidra): mark empty xrefs results as unresolved, not unreferenced (#8831)

* fix(ghidra): mark empty xrefs results as unresolved, not unreferenced

Ghidra 12.2 resolves no references to data addresses on some Mach-O
imports, and xrefs returned a bare empty list with nothing separating
'no references exist' from 'this provider resolved no references', so
callers concluded addresses were unreferenced.

projectExecution now attaches ghidraEmptyXrefsLimitation to an empty
xrefs result: the list reflects what this analysis resolved, not proof
the address is unreferenced. Non-empty results carry no caveat.

Covered by behavior tests for both branches; validated against
FM9-Edit-arm64 (expect: limitation) once the daemon session reopens.

* fix(ghidra): drop circular trace_feature cross-check from empty xrefs caveat

trace_feature calls xrefs internally, so recommending it as an independent
cross-check repeats the same lookup the caveat qualifies. Keep disassembly
as the single independent check.

* fix(ghidra): report actionable-reference absence and invalidate stale snapshots

Review follow-up on the empty xrefs caveat:
- The bridge filters synthetic entry-point references before observation, so
  "resolved no references" could be false; the caveat now reports that no
  actionable references were returned and names the omission.
- Drop the trace_feature cross-check: traceReferences observes xrefs per
  matched string, repeating the same lookup instead of independent evidence.
- Bump instruction_references semantics to v3 so analysis snapshots captured
  before the caveat replay no bare empty results; the profile commitment in
  the snapshot binding no longer matches.

* feat(ghidra): mark empty function-reference facets as unresolved too

Extends the empty-xrefs caveat to the sibling ReferenceManager consumers
review follow-up identified: procedure_references and analyze_function
reference facets built on the same observation path could still present
empty arrays as collected facts.

- ghidraEmptyFunctionReferencesLimitation attaches when
  procedure_references returns no references for the requested direction
  and when a dossier observes no references in either direction;
  callers/callees (function-manager derived, observed working on the
  reported target) stay caveat-free.
- One emptyReferenceCaveat owner replaces the inline xrefs branch.
- function_references semantics bump to v3 so snapshots captured before
  the caveat do not replay bare empty facets; raw profile digests
  recomputed.

* fix(ghidra): cover annotation and instruction reference facets in the caveat

Review follow-up: annotate_native_function returns a dossier built by the
same analyzeFunction collection and inspect_native_instruction builds
incoming_references with visitObservedReferencesTo; both could present
empty arrays as collected facts under the reported ReferenceManager
failure.

- annotate_native_function attaches the caveat when its dossier observes
  no references in either direction.
- inspect_native_instruction attaches it when incoming_references is an
  explicit empty array (null or omission stays unavailable, matching the
  field contract).
- Split the diagnostics describe to keep each block under the lint bound.
- Behavior tests cover attach and non-attach for both operations.

* fix(ghidra): name the honest cross-check limits in the reference caveats

Review follow-up: the motivating failure was a string address, so
'cross-check the disassembly at this address' pointed at nothing — data
and string addresses have no instruction to disassemble — and
inspect_native_instruction's incoming_references is built through the
same visitObservedReferencesTo path, so it was not independent either.

- xrefs caveat now states that no independent in-product cross-check
  exists for the empty result, that surrounding disassembly only helps
  at a code address, and that data or string addresses need an external
  disassembly scan (otool -tV adrp/add pairing).
- Function-facet caveat separates outgoing references (own disassembly
  is independent) from incoming references (no in-product check; scan
  other code externally).

* fix(ghidra): use the address-scoped caveat for inspect_native_instruction

Greptile review follow-up: inspect_native_instruction checks incoming
references to one exact address, so the function-scoped caveat misdescribed
the scope; an instruction can be unreferenced while its function has
references elsewhere, and the address may have no containing function.
Attach the address-scoped xrefs caveat instead.

* fix(ghidra): qualify each empty reference direction independently

Analyze-function and annotate-native-function results attached the
unresolved-references caveat only when BOTH reference directions were
empty, so a dossier with one populated direction presented its empty
direction as a collected fact.

Split the combined function-references caveat into direction-scoped
limitations and attach one per empty direction (analyze_function,
annotate_native_function dossier readback, procedure_references by its
requested direction).

* fix(ghidra): qualify empty outgoing instruction references

inspect_native_instruction results carry two independent
ReferenceManager facets: the incoming list and the outgoing references
built from instruction.getReferencesFrom(). Only the incoming list was
checked, so an instruction with a populated incoming list and no
outgoing references presented the empty outgoing facet as a collected
fact, and any populated incoming list suppressed the caveat entirely.

Each facet is now qualified independently: the empty incoming list
keeps the address-scoped caveat; the empty outgoing list attaches the
new instruction-scoped outgoing limitation (this stream is not
entry-point filtered, so it claims no entry-point omission). Truth
table covered in describe("Ghidra empty instruction reference facets").

* fix(ghidra): gate the instruction outgoing caveat on decoded status

Non-decoded inspect_native_instruction results (data, not-in-listing,
not-instruction-boundary, outside-memory) return before the bridge ever
queries instruction.getReferencesFrom(), so their empty references list
is an unobserved facet, not an empty ReferenceManager observation. The
unconditional outgoing caveat claimed the ReferenceManager returned no
references from an instruction that does not exist at that address.

The outgoing limitation now attaches only when status is decoded; the
address-scoped incoming caveat still applies per the empty incoming
list, matching the original motivating data-address case.

* fix(ghidra): dossier incoming omission and external outgoing recovery

Two unqualified cases remained in the function-reference caveats:

- The analyze_function/annotation dossier excludes incoming references
  whose source is inside the function's own body (a self-recursive call
  is enough), so the projected empty list can mean 'no outside source
  observed' or 'only in-body sources observed'. The dossier now uses a
  dedicated incoming limitation naming the exclusion, pointing at the
  outgoing edges/disassembly where in-body edges remain visible, and at
  procedure_references(incoming) - the same ReferenceManager stream
  without the in-body exclusion - as the in-product discriminator.
  procedure_references keeps the generic incoming caveat: its incoming
  stream is not in-body filtered.

- An external function has no local body, so the outgoing caveat's
  'function's own disassembly' recommendation was impossible. Records
  classified external now get an external-specific outgoing limitation
  naming the defining artifact and this program's call sites instead
  (procedure_references outgoing, analyze_function, annotation readback).

* fix(ghidra): qualify dossier incoming caveat observation

The dossier-specific incoming caveat claimed the ReferenceManager
observed no incoming references from outside the body, but
visitObservedReference (ReaGhidraBridge.java:3973-3974) drops
entry-point references before the body filter (1619-1621), so the
manager may have returned references the dossier never reports.
Reframe as 'returned no actionable' and name both omissions; correct
the recovery claim: procedure_references(incoming) lacks the in-body
filter but omits synthetic entry-point references as well.

commits.subject: fix(ghidra): update the host no-return probe for the current bridge (#8462)
commits.body:
fix(ghidra): update the host no-return probe for the current bridge (#8462)

The host no-return verifier, scripts/verify-real-ghidra-noreturn.mjs,
fails before its Evidence checks. ReaNoReturnProbe calls private bridge
methods through reflection, and two bridge changes left the probe behind:

- d4bd65c53 added a Function parameter to noReturnCallLimitations, and
  225f26a5f renamed the method to functionBoundaryLimitations. The probe
  still looked up noReturnCallLimitations(Iterable) and stopped with
  NoSuchMethodException.
- 01a1b3fda made procedureReferences return a function observation
  envelope. The probe read references and unresolved_calls from the top
  level of that envelope instead of from its value.

Pass each function and its instructions to functionBoundaryLimitations,
and read procedureReferences results from the envelope value. The require
checks are unchanged. CI does not run this verifier.

These edits are the probe repair from robotaro's open draft that treats
demangled C++ runtime imports as returning, copied line for line, so
either change merges cleanly after the other.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): require exactly one fork IPC channel (#8017)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): require exactly one fork IPC channel (#8017)

* fix(javascript): require exactly one fork IPC channel

Node's fork() rejects an explicit stdio array that carries more than one IPC
channel, and the throw is synchronous, before any child process exists:

    if (ArrayPrototypeFilter(options.stdio, ...'ipc').length > 1)
      throw new ERR_IPC_ONE_PIPE()

The analysis already dropped an array with no "ipc" (#7992) but still reported a
resolved fork for an array carrying it twice.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    fork({stdio: ["ipc", "ipc"]})                -> THROWS ERR_IPC_ONE_PIPE
    fork({stdio: ["pipe", "ipc", "ipc"]})        -> THROWS ERR_IPC_ONE_PIPE
    fork({stdio: ["ipc"]})                       -> SPAWNED connected=true
    fork({stdio: ["pipe", "ipc"]})               -> SPAWNED connected=true
    fork({stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe", "ipc"]})-> SPAWNED connected=true

So the required count is exactly one, not at least one. Count the resolved "ipc"
literals and reject the candidate unless the count is one; a spread or an
unreadable element may still change the count and is left alone, as before.

commits.subject: fix(mcp): keep detail guidance in compact input schemas (#8034)
commits.body:
fix(mcp): keep detail guidance in compact input schemas (#8034)

Compact input schemas are the default advertisement since #5975, and the
profile drops every property description. On 23 of the 31 tools with a
guided `detail` option, including inspect_artifact and inspect_macho,
`detail` is advertised as a bare complete|summary enum, so callers take the
complete default. On a universal macOS app that reply was about 699k
characters for inspect_artifact and 336k for inspect_macho, against about
4.4k and 3.2k with summary.

Keep the canonical description of a root `detail` property in the inline
compact input form. The reduced form already keeps first-level guidance, and
compact output schemas are unchanged. Advertised compact input schemas grow
from 127,616 to 133,358 bytes across 233 tools; the largest schema stays at
4,107 bytes, within the 13,312-byte budget.

The new boundary test compares `detail` guidance between the full and compact
tools/list and fails before the change.

commits.subject: fix(node-sea): bound ELF note scans by the notes a carrier holds (#8031)
commits.body:
fix(node-sea): bound ELF note scans by the notes a carrier holds (#8031)

Artifact classification probes every ELF root for a Node SEA note. Each
PT_NOTE program header was scanned on its own, one read per note, so
headers that declare the same note bytes multiplied the work: a 295 KB
ELF with 4,096 such headers kept inspect-artifact busy for about three
and a half minutes.

Every note header takes at least 12 bytes, so disjoint tables hold at
most one note per 12 file bytes. The scan now stops there. Past that
count the remaining tables are unreadable: an ELF without a confirmed
blob keeps its native classification, and a confirmed blob fails closed.

commits.body:
fix(gdb): keep sessions usable after an oversized stream record (#8029)

* fix(gdb): keep sessions usable after an oversized stream record

A single MI console, target or log record over the 16 MiB line limit
failed the whole session protocol, so close could not re-synchronize
and GDB plus its inferior stayed owned with no recovery path.

MI stream records carry only output and c-strings escape newlines, so
a raw LF always ends the record. #receive now drops the remainder of

and async records still fail closed as before.

commits.subject: fix(cli): seal in-process Evidence before publishing (#8468)
commits.body:
fix(cli): seal in-process Evidence before publishing (#8468)

* fix(cli): seal in-process Evidence before publishing

The CLI rebuilt a plain bundle from records it had already authenticated,
so writeEvidenceBundle cloned and authenticated the complete analyzed
graph again at the final checkpoint. On a default heap that second copy
could exceed available memory after minutes of analysis and discard the
whole run.

Seal the in-process bundle once so publication can stream the canonical
form without the redundant authentication copies. The regression test
fails on the previous behavior with resource_constraint under a one-byte
heap allowance.

Fixes #8411

* fix(cli): preserve the heap check for mutable Evidence

Only seal the publication bundle when every record is already immutable.
Mutable producer records keep the writer's existing heap check instead of
being copied before that check. The regression now covers the safe
fallback and lets the shared temporary-directory fixture own cleanup.

* test(cli): keep a distinct mutable source in the publication regression

Seal the main record and give the mutable source its own evidence ID so
the map cannot replace it before the bundle guard runs.

commits.subject: fix(ghidra): keep a changed existing project's refusal typed through launch (#8273)
commits.body:
fix(ghidra): keep a changed existing project's refusal typed through launch (#8273)

* fix(ghidra): keep a changed existing project's refusal typed through launch

When the selected REA_GHIDRA_PROJECT_PATH project changes after
open_binary commits its profile, the launcher's verified copy refuses it
with AnalysisArtifactChangedError. GhidraHeadlessLauncher wraps that in
GhidraLaunchError, and the session error's cause became the wrapper, so
the projection missed the existing artifact_changed branch and returned
generic execution_failure with rea doctor advice.

Read the launcher's primary failure when it is an
AnalysisArtifactChangedError, so the refusal reaches callers as
artifact_changed with the changed path and the existing reopen guidance.
The refusal stays fail-closed: no automatic reopen or fresh-import
fallback. Other launch failures keep their current projection.

Fixes #8217

* fix(ghidra): describe a project profile mismatch without a timing claim

When the owned copy of a selected Ghidra project no longer matches the
fingerprint committed by open_binary, copyExistingGhidraProject threw
RegularFileChangedError, so the artifact_changed reason said the input
"changed while being read". A digest mismatch only shows that the
project differs from its committed profile; the change may have happened
before the copy started.

Throw AnalysisArtifactChangedError directly with a reason that states
the mismatch and leaves the time of the change unestablished. Changes
observed while files are being read keep their existing reason.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): link a response body reader only to a settled fetch (#8028)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): link a response body reader only to a settled fetch (#8028)

* fix(javascript): link a response body reader only to a settled fetch

`collectResponseConsumers` treated any `.json()`/`.text()`/`.arrayBuffer()` on a
binding holding a request result as a response consumer, and gave it the
request's endpoint at `resolution: "complete"`. That holds only for a settled
`fetch`.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    await fetch(u)               -> Response      json/text/arrayBuffer = function
    fetch(u) unawaited           -> Promise       json = undefined; pending.json() THROWS TypeError
    http.get(u)                  -> ClientRequest json/text/arrayBuffer = undefined
    http.request(u)              -> ClientRequest json = undefined; request.text() THROWS TypeError
    new WebSocket(u)             -> WebSocket     socket.json() THROWS TypeError
    await http.get(u)            -> ClientRequest (await does not help)

So four shapes emitted a resolved "this endpoint's body is read here" fact for a
call that throws before any body is read: an un-awaited fetch, `http.get`,
`http.request`, and a `WebSocket` handshake.

Link only requests that settle to a `Response`: a `fetch` call whose value is
awaited through expression wrappers. A binding that also holds a request kind
without a body reader keeps the consumer a candidate (`partial`) rather than a
proven one, and a binding with no settled fetch emits no consumer at all, which
matches the `collectReleases` / `forkRejectsStdioArray` precedent — the receiver
provably has no such member, so there is no fact to report.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): emit no promise for a literal non-callable executor (#8264)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): emit no promise for a literal non-callable executor (#8264)

* fix(javascript): emit no promise for a literal non-callable executor

Node's `Promise` constructor calls the executor synchronously and throws a
`TypeError` when it is not callable, before any promise object exists. The
analysis reported a `constructor` promise operation with a hardcoded
`sourceResolution: "complete"`, which the graph projects as
`creates-promise` `resolved`.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    new Promise()                        -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(1) / (-1)                -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise("work") / (`work`)       -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(true) / (!0)             -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(null) / (void 1)         -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(1n) / (/re/)             -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise([]) / ({})               -> THREW TypeError
    --- accepted ---
    new Promise(() => {})                -> OK Promise
    new Promise(async () => {})          -> OK Promise
    new Promise(function () {})          -> OK Promise
    new Promise(class {})                -> OK Promise

A class passes Node's own `typeof` check, so it keeps its operation. An
identifier, a call result or a spread may still supply a function and also keeps
its operation.

The filter gates the candidate push rather than `promiseCandidateDetails`, which
also decides whether an `await` becomes an `awaited-expression`: gating there
made `await new Promise(1)` emit a spurious task fact, whereas gating at the push
site makes it emit nothing, which is the honest answer.

* chore: retrigger title and readiness checks after the title was corrected

* fix(javascript): reject a non-finite executor, not only a literal

greptile caught that `new Promise(1e309)` still emitted a promise. Babel stores
that literal as `Infinity`, and `readExactJavaScriptLiteral` refuses to price a
non-finite number, so the guard missed it.

Measured on Node 24.22.1 — every one throws before a promise exists:

    new Promise(1e309)     -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(1e400)     -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(Infinity)  -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(-Infinity) -> THREW TypeError
    new Promise(NaN)       -> THREW TypeError

A numeric literal is now read directly rather than through the exact-value
reader. `Infinity` and `NaN` are identifiers rather than literals, so they are
decided through `isUnmodifiedGlobalReference`; a shadowed binding keeps its
promise, which is the same scoping rule the timer fix uses.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): emit no child process for a literal non-object options slot (#8019)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): emit no child process for a literal non-object options slot (#8019)

* fix(javascript): emit no child process for a literal non-object options slot

Node validates the child_process options object before creating anything, so a
literal primitive or a literal array in that slot throws ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
synchronously and no child process exists. The analysis still reported a complete
spawn for them.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    spawn(cmd, "status")        -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], "pipe")      -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], null)        -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], [])          -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    execFile(cmd, "status")     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    fork(worker, "status")      -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    fork(worker, [], "pipe")    -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    --- accepted by Node ---
    spawn(cmd, args, undefined) -> SPAWNED
    spawn(cmd, args, {})        -> SPAWNED
    execFile(cmd, [], null)     -> SPAWNED
    fork(worker, [], null)      -> SPAWNED
    exec(cmd, "inherit")        -> SPAWNED

The asymmetries matter: `spawn` rejects `null` and exempts only `undefined`,
while `fork` and `execFile` skip any nullish options, and `exec` spreads its
options and validates none of them. Drop a candidate only when the options slot
is a provable literal primitive or array, so an unresolved or non-literal value
stays a candidate.

`spawn(cmd, [], null)` is the sharpest case: it was indistinguishable from the
valid `undefined` form, including a resolved connects-stdio relation, for a call
that dies before any child exists.

* chore: retrigger title and readiness checks after the title was corrected

* fix(javascript): reject literal options Node shall reject, and drop a stray file

Two review findings on #8019.

greptile: `rejectsOptionsShape` still kept `spawn("tool", [], 0n)`, `-0` and
`1e400`, which Node also rejects before creating a child
(`ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE: The "options" argument must be of type object`). Those
forms are exactly the ones `readExactJavaScriptLiteral` refuses to price — a
BigInt, a non-finite numeric literal and a negated numeric literal — so read the
shape directly instead of widening the shared exact-value reader. `NaN` is an
identifier rather than a literal, so it still needs scope resolution and is left
as a documented gap.

Also remove `.rea-hopper-stage-YOryZ6/`, a local Hopper installation stub that an
`add -A` swept into the commit. It is unrelated to this change.

* fix(javascript): keep a void options slot, reject ! and ~

greptile flagged that `isUnpricedPrimitiveLiteral` dropped `spawn("tool", [], void 0)`,
`fork(..., void 0)` and `execFile(..., void 0)`. It checked the unary operand without
the operator, but `void <expr>` evaluates to `undefined`, which is the one options
value Node accepts in place of an object.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    spawn(cmd, [], void 0) -> SPAWNED
    spawn(cmd, [], void 5) -> SPAWNED
    spawn(cmd, [], -0)     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], -5)     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], +5)     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], !0)     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn(cmd, [], ~0)     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE

So the operator now decides: `void` keeps the spawn, `!` and `~` reject whatever
their operand, and `+`/`-` reject only when the operand is a numeric literal.

* fix(javascript): reject a non-finite global in the child-process options slot

An unshadowed `NaN` or `Infinity` in the options slot is a number, and Node's
options check rejects a number exactly as it rejects any other primitive. The
guard read only literal nodes, so the global identifier passed through. Measured
on Node 24.22.1:

    spawn("e", NaN)        -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    spawn("e", Infinity)   -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    execFile("e", NaN)     -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    fork("x.js", NaN)      -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    --- accepted ---
    exec("e", NaN)         -> ok, because exec validates no options
    spawn("e", undefined)  -> ok, the one accepted global
    spawn("e", null)       -> ok
    spawn("e", []) / ({})  -> ok

`isUnshadowedGlobal` keeps a local binding named `NaN` out of the rule, so a
shadowed value keeps its fact. Seven regressions cover the rejected forms plus
`exec`, `undefined`, `null`, an array, an object and a shadowed `NaN`; all seven
fail on the previous commit.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): emit no fs acquisition for a literal non-flag string (#8125)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): emit no fs acquisition for a literal non-flag string (#8125)

* fix(javascript): emit no fs acquisition for a literal non-flag string

`fs.open` and `fs.openSync` validate a literal flag before touching the
filesystem:

    if (!isFd(flags) && !FLAGS_SET.has(flags))
      throw new ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE('flags', flags, ...);

The throw is synchronous, before a descriptor exists, but the analysis reported
an `acquire` operation for those calls.

Measured on Node 24.22.1 against a file that does not exist, so each valid flag
is exercised without an EEXIST masking it:

    ACCEPTED as a flags string:
      a a+ as as+ ax ax+ r r+ rs rs+ sa sa+ sr sr+ w w+ wx wx+ xa xa+ xw xw+
    REJECTED with ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE:
      "" A R W rb wb s s+ x r,x

A Python-style `"rb"`/`"wb"` is the common case: those are valid in Python and
fatal at the Node call site.

`FS_OPEN_FLAGS` in `javascriptStaticAnalysisHelpers.ts` already holds exactly
those 22 accepted flags. It is now exported and reused so the accepted set has
one owner. A numeric flag is a platform bitmask and a computed value may still be
valid, so only an exactly readable non-flag string is dropped.

`fs.createReadStream` keeps its acquisition: it does not validate the flag
synchronously, it returns a stream and reports the failure on the error event.

* chore: retrigger title and readiness checks after the title was corrected

* fix(javascript): reject every fs flag literal Node rejects

The first version only decided string flags. Node's check covers every flag
shape, and each one below throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` or `ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE`
synchronously, before a descriptor exists:

    openSync(p, 1.5)      -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, -1)       -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, -1.5)     -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, 1e400)    -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, NaN)      -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, Infinity) -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, 0n)       -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    openSync(p, true)     -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    openSync(p, false)    -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    openSync(p, {})       -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    openSync(p, [])       -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    --- accepted ---
    openSync(p, 0) / 1 / 65536 / +5   -> ok
    openSync(p) / undefined / null    -> ok
    openSync(p, "r") / "wx" / "sr"    -> ok

`NaN` and `Infinity` are identifiers rather than literals, so they are decided
only through `isUnmodifiedGlobalReference`; a shadowed binding keeps the
acquisition.

* fix(javascript): judge an fs flag by its value, and ignore a shifting spread

Two P1 findings on the first version.

**A unary operator was judged by its operand.** `openSync(p, void 1.5)` passes
`undefined`, so Node applies the default read flag, but the branch saw a
fractional operand and dropped a real acquisition. `openSync(p, -0)` is the valid
zero bitmask and was also dropped. `staticFlagBits` now evaluates the operator:

    openSync(p, void 1.5)   -> ok      (keeps the acquisition)
    openSync(p, void 0)     -> ok
    openSync(p, -0)         -> ok
    openSync(p, -0.0)       -> ok
    openSync(p, +0)         -> ok
    openSync(p, ~-1)        -> ok
    openSync(p, -1)         -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, -1.5)       -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, +1.5)       -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, !0)         -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    openSync(p, ~0)         -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, typeof 1)   -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE

**A spread before the flag slot shifts the runtime position.** With
`args = [path, "w"]`, `openSync(...args, "0600")` opens with mode `"0600"`, but
argument 1 is then the mode rather than the flag. The check now keeps the
acquisition whenever argument 0 is a spread, because the flag it inspects is not
provably the flag at runtime.

* fix(javascript): leave a signed fs bitmask undecided

greptile caught that the flag check rejected every negative integer, but Node
accepts some signed bitmasks. Measured on Node 24.22.1 against an existing file:

    openSync(p, -2147483648)   -> ok
    openSync(p, -1073741824)   -> ok
    openSync(p, -1)            -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, -2)            -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, 2147483647)    -> THREW EINVAL
    openSync(p, 2147483648)    -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
    openSync(p, -2147483649)   -> THREW ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE

So the sign does not decide: some negative values open a descriptor and others do
not, and which is which is a platform bitmask question this analysis cannot
settle. The check now rejects only a non-integer or a value outside the signed
32-bit range, and leaves an in-range negative undecided — the same choice
`greptile` asked for, on the principle that a call which may succeed must keep
its acquisition.

`!`, `typeof` and `delete` are still rejected, because those yield a boolean or a
string regardless of the operand.

* fix(javascript): read a no-expression template literal flag

Review finding. A no-expression template literal is exactly readable, so it is the
same flag string Node receives, but the guard only read `StringLiteral`:

    fs.openSync(p, ` + "`rb`" + `)   -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE
    fs.openSync(p, ` + "`r`" + `)    -> ok

The flag slot now accepts an interpolation-free template; an interpolated template
stays undecided.

Four regressions cover both directions; two fail without the change.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): emit no timer for a literal non-function callback (#8044)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): emit no timer for a literal non-function callback (#8044)

* fix(javascript): emit no timer for a literal non-function callback

Node validates the timer callback before creating a handle:

    if (typeof callback !== 'function')
      throw new ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE('callback', 'function', callback);

The throw is synchronous, before any timer exists, but the analysis reported a
`schedule` operation for such calls.

Measured on Node 24.22.1:

    setTimeout("code", 0)    -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(`code`, 0)    -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(1, 0)         -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(1n, 0)        -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(true, 0)      -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(null, 0)      -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(void 0, 0)    -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout([], 0)        -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout({}, 0)        -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout()             -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setImmediate("code")     -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setInterval("code", 0)   -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    --- accepted by Node ---
    setTimeout(function(){}, 0) -> OK
    setTimeout(() => {}, 0)     -> OK
    setTimeout(fn, 0)           -> OK
    setTimeout(class {}, 0)     -> OK (fails only when the class is invoked)

So a schedule is dropped only for an exactly readable literal that is not a
function, or for a missing argument. An identifier, a call result or a spread may
still be a function at runtime and keeps its schedule.

* chore: retrigger title and readiness checks after the title was corrected

* fix(javascript): scope the timer callback rule to Node's timers module

greptile flagged two problems with the first version.

P1 - browser timers disappeared. The rule was applied to bare globals, but
browser and Electron renderer sources reach this analysis without a Node/browser
distinction, and there `setTimeout("refresh()", 0)` is a real timer: the host
evaluates the string. The rule now applies only when the timer is imported from
`node:timers`, where that form cannot exist. A bare global schedule keeps its
fact whatever argument 0 holds.

P2 - unused import. `readExactJavaScriptLiteral` was imported but never used; the
helper reads shapes through `unwrapJavaScriptExpression`. Removed.

Measured on Node 24.22.1 (the throw is what makes a node:timers schedule
impossible; the bare-global case is intentionally left alone):

    import { setTimeout } from "node:timers";
    setTimeout("code", 0)  -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(null, 0)    -> THROWS ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(fn, 0)      -> OK
    --- bare global, host may be a browser ---
    setTimeout("code", 0)  -> kept as a schedule

24 cases cover both sides plus the cancellation link.

* fix(javascript): reject every non-function global and unary timer callback

Reviewing the timer callback guard against Node 24.22.1 found two gaps. Both are
in the same "a call that always throws must not emit a resolved fact" family.

**An unmodified global that is not a function was accepted.** The guard read
literal nodes only, so a bare global identifier passed through even though Node
rejects it before creating a handle:

    setTimeout(undefined)  -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(NaN)        -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(Infinity)   -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE

`isUnmodifiedGlobalReference` keeps a shadowed binding out of the rule, so a
local `const NaN = () => {}` keeps its schedule.

**Only `void` was treated as a non-function unary operator.** Every unary operator
yields a primitive, and Node rejects a primitive callback:

    setTimeout(!0)         -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(~0)         -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(-1)         -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(+"1")       -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE
    setTimeout(typeof 1)   -> THREW ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE

A class expression is still kept, because it passes Node's own `typeof` check and
only fails when invoked.

Fifteen regressions cover the rejected forms plus arrow, identifier, class,
spread and shadowed-global cases; ten fail on the previous commit.

* fix(javascript): let sloppy eval shadow the non-function global callback

Review finding. The new global check read `undefined`, `NaN` and `Infinity` as
unmodified globals, but sloppy `eval` can introduce a local function under one of
those names, which then shadows the global. Measured on Node 24.22.1 in script
scope:

    function g() { eval("var undefined = () => {}"); setTimeout(undefined, 0); }
    -> schedules a timer
    function g() { eval("var NaN = () => {}"); setTimeout(NaN, 0); }
    -> schedules a timer

`semanticOpaqueNameMayHaveChanged` now has to agree that no visible activation can
introduce such a name before the global reading is conclusive. In a module the
same `eval` is strict and introduces no outer binding, so the global reading still
holds and the timer is still dropped.

Three regressions cover the sloppy forms, and a fourth pins the no-eval cases as
still dropped. The three sloppy cases fail without the guard.

commits.subject: fix(native): select versioned arm64e slices for codesign by family name (#8713)
commits.body:
fix(native): select versioned arm64e slices for codesign by family name (#8713)

* fix(native): select versioned arm64e slices for codesign by family name

Current clang marks arm64e slices with pointer-authentication ABI
version 1 (subtype 0x81000002, lipo name arm64e.v1). The codesign
selector table accepted only ABI version 0, so inspect-signature failed
with capability_unavailable whenever such a slice was selected, for
example on any universal arm64e + x86_64 binary built today.

codesign has no versioned name: -a arm64e.v1 is "unknown architecture
name", and -a arm64e resolves to the first FAT slice with the arm64e
base subtype, whatever its ABI version. A selector is therefore exact
only for that first slice. Accept any versioned pointer-authentication
ABI for arm64e, and return a selector only when the slice is the first
in table order to carry that name; a later slice sharing it stays
unknown instead of being inspected through the earlier one. This also
removes the separate duplicate-name check from signature coverage.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(native): keep arm64e selectors unknown behind unmapped variants

codesign resolves a name to the first FAT slice with the same CPU type and
base subtype, so an earlier capability variant whose own name is unknown may
shadow a later arm64e slice. Compare identities rather than successful name
mappings.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: fix(firmware): reject staged files cut off at the per-file limit (#4430)
commits.body:
fix(firmware): reject staged files cut off at the per-file limit (#4430)

* fix(firmware): keep producer reports writable under small staging budgets

extract_firmware passed max_output_bytes straight to prlimit --fsize. RLIMIT_FSIZE
applies to every regular file the producer writes, including the mandatory
report.json and unblob.log outside the staging tree, so a staging budget smaller
than the report truncated it and failed the extraction even when every staged
file fit. Derive the per-file ceiling as the larger of the staging budget and the
8 MiB report budget; polling and the final inventory still enforce the aggregate
staging budget.

Fixes #3888

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(firmware): keep files stopped at the size ceiling over budget

The per-file RLIMIT_FSIZE ceiling equalled the largest size its readers
accept, and both the staging inventory and the report reader accept a
file of exactly their budget. A write the kernel stopped at the ceiling
therefore left a truncated file that passed as complete. Raise the
ceiling by one byte so such a file exceeds its budget and is rejected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(firmware): report the effective file-size ceiling on limit failures

The exit path re-derived the staging budget for SIGXFSZ and process-limit
recovery, so a small-budget run killed at the 8 MiB + 1 ceiling reported
file_size_bytes 64 and said the cap was max_output_bytes. Pass the
ceiling runFirmwareCommand installs and describe how it is derived.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(firmware): reject staged files cut off at the per-file limit

RLIMIT_FSIZE stops a write at the limit without extending the file, and
the staging inventory admits a file of exactly max_output_bytes. With a
budget of 8 MiB or more the producer limit equalled the budget, so a
staged file the kernel cut short published as a complete extraction;
an inherited ceiling below the budget did the same.

Derive the per-run limit once in firmwareFileSizeLimit as one byte above
the largest budget, still capped by the inherited ceiling, so a file
stopped at the limit exceeds its budget. When the inherited ceiling
removes that byte, both staging inventories refuse a regular file that
reaches the installed limit with a nonretryable file-size constraint
naming the inherited limit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(firmware): derive limit adjustability from the per-run limit

The one byte of headroom makes the per-run file limit equal an
inherited ceiling of exactly max_output_bytes + 1, but adjustability
still compared that ceiling with the raw budget. A SIGXFSZ then advised
raising max_output_bytes, which the same ceiling clamps back to the
same limit.

Decide adjustability in firmwareFileSizeAdjustable from
firmwareFileSizeLimit itself: recommend a larger budget only when it
raises that limit.

branch, check that the two branches stay distinct, and compare the inventory
refusal with firmwareFileSizeLimitReached. The selected limit, resource and

commits.subject: fix(artifacts): decide how compare_artifacts compares every format_metadata kind (#8231)
commits.body:
fix(artifacts): decide how compare_artifacts compares every format_metadata kind (#8231)

* feat(artifacts): inventory and extract ESP32 firmware images

ESP32-family app and bootloader images (magic 0xE9) had no reader, so
open_binary refused OTA downloads, app partitions and bootloaders.

Add the esp-image container format behind inspect_artifact and
extract_artifact. A pure decoder reads each byte once and keeps only
fixed-size fields. Derived facts cover the chip, from a table cited to
ESP-IDF v6.1; segment classification as ESP-IDF's should_map and
should_load; checksum and appended SHA-256 results; app and bootloader
descriptors; Secure Boot v2 signature blocks, observed and unverified;
and undescribed trailing byte ranges. Truncation and undescribed bytes
make coverage unknown. ESP8266 images are refused with a specific
reason, and ciphertext stays unrecognized.

Add the format to every target, Evidence, snapshot, live-summary and
artifact vocabulary, document it, and add an optional verify:esp-images
lane that compares esptool-built images with esptool image-info and
espsecure signature-info-v2.

Refs #3615

* test(artifacts): run the ESP image lane on esptool v5.6.0

The lane compared descriptor fields only when esptool image-info printed
one, so a descriptor that REA reports and esptool does not print passed
without comparison. Compare the descriptor kind in both directions.

Record that the lane passed for all 13 images with esptool and espsecure
v5.6.0, the version the layout facts cite, as well as with 4.12.0.

* refactor(artifacts): define ESP image layout sizes once

The decoder and the derived facts each defined the segment-header,
appended-digest and flash-sector sizes, the erased-byte scan and the
offset formatter. Define them once with the other fixed-layout structures
and import them in both places. The signature slot count is the one
constant that drives the slot scan.

Correct the observedEnd comment: it is the end of the last chunk read.

* fix(artifacts): report ESP-IDF's segment length limit by chip

ESP-IDF's verify_segment_header rejects a segment of 16 MiB or more
unless the chip maps flash through 32-bit cache addresses
(SOC_SPI_MEM_SUPPORT_CACHE_32BIT_ADDR_MAP: ESP32-S3, P4, C5, C61, H4 and
S31 in v6.1). Record that capability in the chip table and add a
limitation for such segments; unknown chips get none.

`loaded` repeats should_load. It does not mean the bootloader accepts the
segment: verify_load_addresses still rejects one outside the chip's RAM,
which REA does not model. Say so in the docs, the skill reference and the
inventory limitation.

* test(artifacts): check ESP lane tools first and verify extraction

The lane started work before checking its tools, so a missing RISC-V
target, ld.lld, esptool or espsecure surfaced as a raw spawn or command
error. Check each one before building and name the variable to set. Warn
when esptool is not v5.6.0, the release the layout facts cite.

Assert each segment's class for the ESP32-C3 app, its variants and the
bootloader, as the Xtensa image already did. Extract the app and the
signed image through the CLI and compare every file with the bytes at
esptool's segment offsets or in the appended signature sector; the
source's SHA-256 must be unchanged and equal the reported root_sha256.

* docs(artifacts): state what the ESP image lane does not establish

The Verification section listed the lane's checks but not its gaps: only
ESP32-C3 and ESP32 images come from a real producer, no real project
build, OTA download or flash dump is inspected, no signature is verified,
and the lane does not run in CI.

Record the timing of the final lane run on esptool v5.6.0.

* fix(artifacts): compare ESP segment declarations

Segment entries hash only their data, so compare_artifacts reported a
segment that moved to another load address with the same bytes as
unchanged; only the image itself changed. Compare each segment's
load_addr and data_len as its declaration, as Node SEA and PyInstaller
members are compared, and count a changed declaration as a metadata
change, also when content is unavailable.

Header offsets are layout and the classification is derived, so neither
is compared.

* test(artifacts): run ESP lane commands as owned process trees

The lane ran its tools through execFile. A timeout killed only the direct
child, so a linker or assembler that Clang or GCC had started could keep
running while the lane removed its workspace. Run every command through
createVerifierCommands, check the tools inside withVerifierCleanup, and
remove the workspace only after commands.close() has stopped every tree;
a failed close keeps the workspace.

Only a nonzero exit now counts as a refusal or an expected esptool
failure; timeouts and spawn failures propagate. Supervising each command
roughly doubles the lane's run time.

* test(artifacts): cancel ESP decoding after its first decoded chunk

The cancellation test requested cancel or close on setImmediate, which
can land while the file is still being opened and checked, so it never
showed that decoding had started. It also passed against a reader that
ignored both requests while decoding. Acknowledge the decoder's first
chunk, then cancel or close, join the operation, and assert that no
later chunk reaches the decoder and that the reader ends closed.

* docs(artifacts): record which ESP metadata comparison ignores

Segments are compared by their declaration. The image's and the
signature blocks' format_metadata are not: every field comes from their
own bytes, which content comparison already covers, and a block's
image_digest_matches follows the image's content.

* fix(artifacts): decide declaration comparison for every metadata kind

compare_artifacts listed the format_metadata kinds it compared by hand,
so a new kind went uncompared without notice; ESP segment load addresses
were first missed this way. One table beside the schemas now gives every
kind a declaration projection or the reason comparison uses none of its
facts, and a kind without an entry does not compile. Consumers read one
result per pair instead of naming formats.

- Godot PCK entries stay uncompared. Godot looks members up by the
  simplified path without res://, which logical_path holds apart from
  Unicode normalization. Godot 4.3 exports store res:// and 4.4.1
  exports do not, so comparing source_path would mark every member
  changed. The reader admits only the encryption flag, which the
  occurrence's encrypted field records.
- A changed PyInstaller declaration is now a metadata change also when
  the member's content is unavailable, as for ASAR, Node SEA and ESP
  segments. It was unknown before, for no recorded reason.
- Root kinds and ESP signature blocks stay uncompared: their fields come
  from their own bytes, which content comparison covers.
- A declaration that only one side records now adds one generic
  limitation for every compared kind. Only Node SEA added one before,
  with its own text.

* fix(artifacts): keep content comparison for metadata records with content

The record rule compared two metadata occurrences by their declaration
alone. A hand-built record that names content, with an equal declaration,
then hid a content change; PyInstaller records already did so before the
table. The rule now needs both records without an artifact_id, which is
every metadata record a reader emits.

Review changes in the same area:

- The unknown-declaration limitation also covers declarations of different
  kinds and non-container observations, and tests compare it with its
  constant.
- docs/godot-pck.md gives each Godot version's lookup path, the backslash
  case, and that a member that becomes encrypted compares unknown. The
  table points to it instead of restating it.
- The PyInstaller regression moves to an acceptance test whose MCP client
  validates the advertised output schema, and the domain tests keep one
  representative case per behavior.

* fix(artifacts): compare encryption changes when content is unavailable

An encrypted member has no content. Comparison then took the
content-unavailable fallback, which counted only ASAR storage and format
declarations, so a Godot PCK, ZIP or PYZ member that became encrypted
compared unknown although both sides record `encrypted`. The record rule
compared node-less metadata records by format declaration alone, so a PYZ
namespace record whose encryption flipped compared unchanged.

`OccurrenceMetadata` now owns the encryption comparison beside ASAR
storage and the format declaration. Every occurrence records `encrypted`,
so a pair's comparison is never unknown. The fallback, the record rule and
the metadata dimension read it there; `metadataChanged` no longer compares
`encrypted` itself. The record rule compares all of `OccurrenceMetadata`:
a changed value is changed in metadata, with availability when another is
unknown.

Decision: occurrence limitations still do not count for node-less
records. Readers derive them from the declared facts (the PYZ caveat
follows `encrypted`), and their wording can change between REA versions
while the record stays the same. The fallback does not compare them
either.

Behavior changes:
- A pair with unavailable content whose `encrypted` differs is changed
  [metadata, availability], not unknown [availability].
- A node-less record whose `encrypted` differs is changed [metadata], not
  unchanged.
- A hand-built node-less record that records ASAR storage now compares
  it; no reader emits such records.

Remaining:
- The fallback still ignores `entry_kind` and `executable`, which readers
  also declare, so a file that becomes a symlink, or a mode change on an
  encrypted ZIP member, still compares unknown. `executable` has its own
  dimension, so its fix needs content-free checks split from node checks.
  Each is its own behavior decision.
- Node-bearing pairs still compare limitation wording; records do not.
  Whether limitation wording is ever a comparison fact needs one decision.

* fix(artifacts): compare entry kind and executable when content is unavailable

When either side lacked verified content, comparison took a fallback that
counted only ASAR storage, encryption and format declarations. It compared
`entry_kind` only in the metadata check of pairs with content, and
`executable` only beside the node checks. A ZIP member that became a
symlink, whose target REA does not read, and an encrypted ZIP member whose
Unix mode gained an execute bit therefore compared unknown, although
readers declare both fields on every occurrence.

`OccurrenceMetadata` now owns the entry kind comparison beside encryption;
it is never unknown. Comparison checks fall into two groups: declared facts
that need no content (`executable` and the metadata declarations), and
facts that need both content nodes (content, kind, format, size, relations
and node metadata). The fallback, the record rule and pairs with content
share the declared checks and one rule for unknown declarations. Kind and
format stay content checks: without content they are guesses from the path.

Behavior changes:
- Unless both sides have content, a pair whose entry kind differs is
  changed [metadata, availability], not unknown [availability].
- Such a pair whose `executable` differs is changed [executable,
  availability], with metadata when another declared fact also differs.
- A hand-built node-less record whose `executable` differs is changed
  [executable]. No reader emits such records.

Remaining: declared sizes and integrity digests still compare only through
observed bytes, so they do not count when content is unavailable.

* fix(artifacts): never mark a symlink executable

On POSIX hosts the directory reader recorded a symlink's own permission
bits as `executable`. Linux reports 0777 for every symlink and macOS
usually 0755, so directory, app bundle and DMG symlinks read true. zip.js,
the PyInstaller reader and the Windows branch record false. The previous
commit compares `executable` without content, so a symlink that two
readers or two hosts record differently compared changed in `executable`,
and a non-executable file that became a symlink also reported `executable`.

`hostExecutableMarking` now gives a symlink no marking on any host:
running a symlink runs its target, and the link's own bits do not control
that.

Behavior change: directory, app bundle and DMG inventories record
`executable: false` for symlinks. Occurrence IDs do not change, but the
graph digests and manifest IDs of inventories with symlinks do. Comparing
an inventory stored before this change with a new one therefore reports
changed [executable, availability] once for each such symlink.

* fix(artifacts): stop comparing limitation wording

Pairs with content compared node and occurrence limitations as metadata,
while node-less records, the content-unavailable fallback and inventory
limitations did not. Limitations explain what an observation could
establish. Readers mostly derive them from fields that comparison already
reads, from other occurrences or from what REA could read, and their
wording changes between REA versions. So adding `A` beside an unchanged
ZIP member `a` marked `a` changed in metadata through its case-collision
note, and an older and a newer inventory of equal bytes could differ
wherever a reader reworded a note.

No comparison path reads limitations now. Inventory limitations still
appear in the result, and occurrence limitations stay in the inventory
Evidence. Readers write no node limitations, so only hand-built inventories
compared them.

Behavior change: for a pair with content, limitation text no longer adds
metadata. A pair that differs only there compares unchanged, or unknown
[availability] when a declaration is unknown.

Remaining: a few facts appear only in limitation text, or also in fields
that comparison does not read, so their changes are no longer reported
while the compared bytes stay equal: an ASAR block integrity table or an
unsupported integrity declaration, a Godot member's all-zero MD5, a ZIP
name's leading `./` (also in `source_path`), and a PyInstaller PYZ image
digest (also in `pyz_sha256`; the archive root still reports the change).
Each needs a field or a comparison decision of its own if it matters.

* fix(artifacts): compare declared digests when content is unavailable

Without observed bytes on both sides, comparison ignored the containers'
declared integrity claims. Two encrypted Godot PCK members therefore
compared unknown even when their declared MD5s showed that the script had
changed. Godot's exporter stores the MD5 of a member's original bytes, so
the MD5 does not depend on the encryption IV. This comes from the 4.3,
4.4.1 and 4.7.1 exporter sources; no real encrypted export was compared.

When either side has no content, claims of one algorithm that differ now
make the path changed in metadata and availability. Equal claims add no
change, because they are unverified, and observed bytes still decide when
both sides have them. Godot PCK and ASAR readers record such claims.

For a readable member, a directory that declares or omits an MD5 only
decides whether REA can check its bytes, so such a member compares
unchanged. An encrypted member with an MD5 on only one side stays unknown.

Remaining: declared sizes still compare only through observed bytes.

* docs(artifacts): check the contract's compared kinds against the table

docs/mcp-contracts.md named the format_metadata kinds that
compare_artifacts compares in prose, by hand, so a kind added to the
declaration table could go unnamed. The integration branch already omits
esp-flash-partition, which the ESP flash layout branch adds to the table.

The paragraph now names each compared kind by its identifier. A
conformance test requires it to name exactly the kinds whose table entry
has a declaration, which artifactFormatMetadata.ts exports as
COMPARED_FORMAT_METADATA_KINDS, and no kind that comparison ignores.

* test(artifacts): share the comparison acceptance MCP fixture

Six artifact comparison acceptance tests each copied the same MCP
steps: open_binary, inspect_artifact, the inventory_artifact substep
Evidence, then compare_artifacts. The coverage test repeated the
inspect steps three times and kept its own inventory lookup.

tests/fixtures/artifactComparisonMcp.ts now owns these steps on the
schema-validating connectLocalToolsMcp client.
connectArtifactComparisonMcp() returns call, inspect(path) and
compare(left, right). inventoryEvidence() reads the inventory Evidence
that an inspection retains, from MCP or CLI output. Each test still
writes its own authored input and keeps its expectations.

The coverage lookup matched evidence.operation, not the substep
operation. The inspection schema fixes both to inventory_artifact, so
both select the same substep.

The plist acceptance test does not change. It compares the inspection
Evidence itself across CLI and MCP and passes the comparison Evidence
to verify_reconstruction and find_changed_behavior.

No assertion or scenario changes.

* fix(artifacts): leave .NET bundle member declarations uncompared

Upstream main compares no .NET bundle member facts. Comparing `file_type`
changed `compare_artifacts` output beyond this branch's fixes, so the kind
stays uncompared until that is decided. A changed manifest still shows as a
content change of the host.

* fix(artifacts): leave HEX region declarations uncompared

The comparison table compared a region's start_address and length. A
region's path names its start and end addresses, and its length follows
from them, so two regions that pair at one path always declare the same
facts: the entry could never find a change. It only made a region with
equal bytes unknown when the other side recorded no metadata, such as a
directory of extracted regions. The kind is not compared, as on main.

The contract paragraph also stops naming .NET bundle members, which
3e51a7760 left uncompared.

* test(artifacts): compare node-less records of any compared kind

The record rule follows the comparison table, not PyInstaller, but only
PyInstaller records exercised it. An ESP segment record shows both
outcomes: an equal declaration compares unchanged and a moved one changed
in metadata, without the availability that the fallback for unread
content would add.

* test(artifacts): compare a node-less record's recorded ASAR storage

The record rule compares ASAR storage beside the declaration and
`encrypted`, but no test recorded it on a metadata record. A changed
value is changed in metadata, and a value that only one side records
is unknown in availability, as for any occurrence.

* test(artifacts): compare UnityFS member declarations through MCP

The table compares a UnityFS member's declared source_path and raw
flags, but no comparison test covered the kind, so dropping either field
from the projection left every test passing. Bundles with equal member
bytes now show both: other flags, or a stored path in decomposed form,
compare changed in metadata, and reordered members, whose index and
stream offset are layout, compare unchanged.

* test(artifacts): use the shared comparison fixture for UnityFS

The UnityFS comparison test arrived from the bottom branch with its own
copy of the open_binary, inspect_artifact and compare_artifacts steps,
which tests/fixtures/artifactComparisonMcp.ts owns here. It now uses
connectArtifactComparisonMcp() like the other comparison acceptance
tests. No assertion changes.

* test(artifacts): find the contract's compared kinds by marker

The docs conformance test found its paragraph by an exact English phrase,
so rewording "also compares" failed it while the named kinds stayed
right. The paragraph now sits between BEGIN and END markers, as the
allocation report's sections do, and the test reads the kinds between
them. It still requires exactly the kinds whose table entry has a
declaration.
